desc:
Sort all suffixes of s in dictionary order. For each pair of neighbouring suffixes in this sorted list, compute the length of their longest common prefix. Return these n - 1 numbers in order: entry k is the common prefix length of the k-th and the (k+1)-th smallest suffix (0-indexed). For a string of length 1 the result is an empty array.

s = "banana"
sorted suffixes: a, ana, anana, banana, na, nana
result = [1,3,0,0,2]
(a|ana share "a"; ana|anana share "ana"; anana|banana share nothing; banana|na nothing; na|nana share "na")
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Build the sorted list of suffixes, then compare each neighbouring pair character by character. That is correct; think about how large the total comparison work can be for "aaaa...".
Process the suffixes in text order (start index 0, 1, 2, ...) instead of sorted order, and remember the LCP value h you found for the previous start index.
Kasai's observation: if suffix i has LCP h with its predecessor in sorted order, then suffix i+1 has an LCP of at least h - 1 with its own predecessor. So keep h and only decrease it by 1 per step.
editorial: First get the suffix array (here by prefix doubling, O(n log2 n)), and the inverse array rank[sa[k]] = k. Comparing every neighbouring pair from scratch can cost O(n2) in total for text such as all a's.

Kasai's algorithm visits the start indices in text order. For suffix i with sorted predecessor j, extend h while characters match, record lcp[rank[i]-1] = h, then decrease h by one for suffix i+1. Why this works: removing the first character of both suffixes i and j leaves suffixes i+1 and j+1 that share h - 1 characters and where j+1 sorts before i+1, so the real predecessor of i+1 shares at least that much. h grows at most 2n times in total, hence O(n) after the suffix array.
